## Interpretations of Probability

Why do we model anything as random?
What does "probability" mean in the real world?

1) <u>Long-run frequency over repeated trials</u>
   **Ex.** repeatedly flipping a coin
   shooting electrons at a double slit
   "you can never step into the same river twice"

2) <u>Systematic random sampling from a population</u>
   **Ex.** survey of 500 random voters
   random assignment to treatment/control
   Randomness comes from experimenter's actions

3) <u>Subjective uncertainty about an outcome</u>
   chance that...
   - President Biden is re-elected
   - Higgs boson has a given mass
   - $P=NP$
   - $100^{th}$ digit of $\pi$ is 5
   Could be broad intersubjective agreement

These are often intertwined:
**Ex.** What if survey sampling is pseudo-random?
Probably relying on shared ignorance

## Where does $\Lambda$ come from?

(Bayesian rejoinder: Where does $P$ come from?)

Four main sources for prior on $\theta$

### <u>Source #1: Subjective beliefs</u>

<u>Pro</u>: Brings all relevant info. to bear
Straightforward interp. of posterior

<u>Con</u>: Posterior is therefore subjective
Embarrassing to write "I think" in abstract
Hard if $\theta$ high-dim or $P$ nonparametric

<u>Ex</u>: Flip coin 20 times, get 7 heads
0.5 probably a better estimate than 0.35
My subjective prior on coins:

$\lambda(\theta)$
|
|        _
|       | |
|       | |
|   _   | |   _
|_|_|_|_|_|_|_|_ $\theta$
0      0.5      1

## Why not always be Bayesian?

**Ex.** $X_1, ..., X_n \overset{iid}{\sim} p$ , $p$ unknown density on $\mathbb{R}$

<u>Estimand</u>: $m = \text{median}(p)$

<u>Estimator</u> $\delta(X) = \text{median}(X)$
- good estimator : robust, nonparametric
- large $n$: $\delta(X) \approx \mathcal{N}(m, (4 n p(m))^{-1})$
- not Bayes for any realistic prior

<u>Bayes approach</u>
- **Step 1.** Define prior over $p$ (infinite-dim!)
- **Step 2.** Calculate posterior
  - Horrific unless we pick special prior
- **Step 3.** Return e.g. $\mathbb{E}[m \mid X]$

If it differs substantially from $\text{median}(X)$, do we trust it?

## Source #2: "Objective" or "vague" prior

Using default prior removes subjectivity
(But then what does the posterior mean?)

### Flat prior
$\lambda(\theta) \propto_{\theta} 1 \quad \text{on } \Theta$
"Indifference" (in $\theta$ parameterization)
Often **improper** $(\Lambda(\Theta) = \infty)$ but usually ok

**Ex:** $\theta \sim$ flat prior on $\mathbb{R}$
$X|\theta \sim N(\theta, \sigma^2)$
$$
\begin{aligned}
\lambda(\theta|x) &\propto_{\theta} p_{\theta}(x) \\
&= \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-(x-\theta)^2/2\sigma^2} \\
&\propto_{\theta} N(x, \sigma^2)
\end{aligned}
$$

$\Lambda([\theta, \theta+\varepsilon]) \quad (\text{Hw } 5)$
$\quad \approx \varepsilon \lambda(\theta) \propto \varepsilon \sqrt{J(\theta)}$
$\quad \quad \approx \sqrt{D_{kl}(P_{\theta} \| P_{\theta+\varepsilon})}$

### Jeffreys prior
$\lambda(\theta) \propto_{\theta} |J(\theta)|^{1/2}$
Higher density where $P_{\theta}$ "changing faster"
Invariant to parameterization

**Ex.** $X|\theta \sim \text{Binom}(n, \theta)$
$\lambda(\theta) \propto_{\theta} J(\theta)^{1/2} = \left( \frac{n}{\theta(1-\theta)} \right)^{1/2} \propto_{\theta} \text{Beta}(\frac{1}{2}, \frac{1}{2})$

$\lambda(\theta) \to \infty$ as $\theta \to 0$ or $1$:
(33x)
$D_{KL}(0.001 \| 0.01) \gg D_{KL}(0.49 \| 0.5)$
$7n \cdot 10^{-3} \quad \quad \quad \quad 2n \cdot 10^{-4}$

## Intersubjective Agreement

Data may effectively rule out most $\theta$ values
$\rightsquigarrow$ Makes posterior uncontroversial

**Ex.** $X \sim \text{Binom}(10^4, \theta)$, observe $X=3000$
$SD_{\theta}(x/n) = \sqrt{\frac{\theta(1-\theta)}{n}} \le 0.005$
$\Rightarrow \text{Lik}(\theta; X) \approx 0$ outside $C = [0.29, 0.31]$
All "reasonable" priors may be $\approx$ flat on $C$
$$
\begin{aligned}
\Rightarrow \lambda(\theta|x) &\tilde{\propto}_{\theta} \text{Lik}(\theta; X) \\
&\tilde{\propto}_{\theta} \exp \left\{ -\frac{J(0.3)}{2} (\theta - 0.3)^2 \right\} \\
&\propto_{\theta} N(0.3, J(0.3)^{-1})
\end{aligned}
$$

Data "swamps" everyone's prior

## Gaussian sequence model

$X|\theta \sim N_d(\mu, I_d) \quad \quad \mu \in \mathbb{R}^d$
Jeffreys prior is flat: $\lambda(\mu) \propto_{\mu} 1$
$\lambda(\mu|x) = N_d(X, I_d) \Rightarrow \mathbb{E}[\mu|x] = X$
Same as UMVU

What about $\rho^2 = \|\mu\|^2$? Recall
$\mu \sim N_d(X, I_d) \Rightarrow \mathbb{E}[\|\mu\|^2 | X] = \|X\|^2 + d$

Note $\delta_{umvu}(x) = \|X\|^2 - d \Rightarrow \delta_{\lambda}(x) = \delta_{umvu}(x) + 2d$
$$
\begin{aligned}
MSE(\theta; \delta_{\lambda}) &= \text{Var}_{\theta}(\delta_{\lambda}) + \text{Bias}_{\theta}(\delta_{\lambda})^2 \\
&= \text{Var}_{\theta}(\delta_{umvu}) + 4d^2
\end{aligned}
$$

What went wrong? Examine Jeffreys prior:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(\rho^2 \le t) &= \text{Vol}(\text{Ball of radius } \sqrt{t}) \\
&= \text{const}(d) \cdot t^{d/2}
\end{aligned}
$$
$\Rightarrow \lambda(\rho^2) \propto_{\rho^2} (\rho^2)^{\frac{d}{2}-1} = \rho^{d-2}$
Grows rapidly! Prior "expects" $\rho^2$ to be huge

## Source #3: Prior or concurrent experience

May have many "copies" of same problem
Assume corresp. $\theta$ values drawn from a population
$\rightsquigarrow$ Hierarchical Bayes / empirical Bayes
Can be hard to choose right reference class

**Ex.** Estimate same-side bias for $m=48$ coin flippers
Flipper $i$ has $n_i$ trials, "true" same-side prob $\theta_i$

### Hierarchical model:
flippers $i=1, \dots, m$
"hyperparameters" $\alpha, \beta \sim \lambda \leftarrow$ "hyperprior"
$\theta_i | \alpha, \beta \overset{iid}{\sim} \text{Beta}(\alpha, \beta)$
$X_i | \alpha, \beta, \theta \overset{ind.}{\sim} \text{Binom}(n_i, \theta_i)$

$\mathbb{E}[\theta_i | X, \alpha, \beta] = \frac{X_i + \alpha}{n_i + \alpha + \beta}$
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[\theta_i | X] &= \mathbb{E} [ \mathbb{E}[\theta_i | X, \alpha, \beta] | X] \\
&= \iint \frac{X_i + \alpha}{n_i + \alpha + \beta} \lambda(\alpha, \beta | X) d\alpha d\beta
\end{aligned}
$$

If $m$ large $\alpha, \beta$ may be "almost known"
$\rightsquigarrow$ choice of $\lambda$ doesn't matter much

## Flexibility of Bayes

Any $\Lambda, \mathcal{P}, L, g(\theta) : \delta_\Lambda$ defined straightforwardly

$$\delta_\Lambda(x) = \underset{d}{\text{argmin}} \int L(\theta, d) \lambda(\theta | x) d\theta$$

Problem reduced to (possibly hard) computation

Posterior is "one stop shop" for all answers

No need for:
- special family structure (exp. fam. / complete s.s.)
- special estimator ($u$-estimable)
- convex or nice $L$

$\implies$ Highly expressive modeling & estimation

Caveat: Limited by ability to do computations
(Topic of next lecture)

## Source #4: Convenience Priors

Choosing conjugate or other "nice" priors
$\leadsto$ much faster computations esp. in high-dim.
